content.title: About
content.content: Bisque is a rich, creamy soup first recorded in culinary literature in 1913. It is traditionally made from shellfish (often crab, shrimp or lobster), vegetables, cream, and aromatic herbs. The result is a velvety texture and a deep, briny flavor.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The earliest published bisque recipe appeared in a French culinary journal in 1913.
Bisque is traditionally served in small ceramic cups, sometimes accompanied by a slice of bread.
The original recipe used only fresh crab meat, but later versions incorporated lobster and scallops.
Garnishes often include a swirl of cream, fresh herbs, and a dash of lemon juice.
In the early 20th century bisque was considered a dish of the elite and featured at aristocratic banquets.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Shellfish used in bisque provide high‑quality protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Source of omega‑3 fatty acids
items.content: Crab and lobster contain omega‑3s that support heart and vascular health.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Bisque supplies vitamin B12 and niacin, important for nervous system function and metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: The soup delivers zinc, selenium and iodine, which aid thyroid function and immune health.

items.title: Easy to digest
items.content: Its smooth consistency makes bisque gentle on the stomach, suitable for people with digestive sensitivities.

items.title: Shellfish allergy
items.content: Bisque can trigger severe allergic reactions in individuals sensitive to crustaceans or mollusks.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Traditional recipes often use broth and soy sauce, raising salt levels; people with hypertension should monitor portions.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Cream and butter make bisque calorie‑rich; moderation is advised for weight‑controlled diets.

items.title: Potential toxins
items.content: Some shellfish can contain histamine; freshness of ingredients is critical.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve bisque hot in small portion cups. Garnish with a drizzle of cream, chopped parsley, or lemon zest. Accompany with crusty baguette slices or croutons.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store leftover bisque in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2 days. Reheat gently over low heat while stirring to prevent the cream from separating.
